Why? Because its a symptom of a bigger problem?

Dams built in the TVA era have a shelf life of only 50 years. Over that time the ground under the dam literally changes shape too much for the dam to stay stable while holding back a wall of water.

What's going on with this one is that the emergency spillway is being eroded from below and the water levels are over-topping the dam. Embankment dams (made of rocks instead of concrete) are made of a clay core surrounded by coarser grained soil and rocks. The clay blocks water, and the larger rocks/soil layers protect the clay from being carried off by the water. Since there isn't much flow at the dam walls this isn't a problem. Once the dam is over-topped though there is a flow that can pick up sediment from underneath the rock layers, erode the clay layer (making it unstable) and the whole thing collapses sending millions of gallons of water downstream.

California will end up demanding more water from their upriver suppliers. It's a problem that'll end up affecting about a dozen states.
